claim: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are broad spectrum antibiotics that selectively target bacteria.
source: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are broad spectrum antibiotics that selectively target bacteria.
evidence: This is a general statement about AMPs that draws from established scientific consensus.

claim: E. coli cells exhibit rapid absorption and retention of a large number of LL37 peptides upon inhibition of their growth.
source: We observe an unexpected, rapid absorption and retention of a large number of LL37 peptides by E. coli cells upon the inhibition of their growth, which increases population survivability.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations described in the abstract and detailed in the results section with single-cell microscopy data.

claim: The absorption of LL37 peptides increases population survivability of E. coli.
source: We observe an unexpected, rapid absorption and retention of a large number of LL37 peptides by E. coli cells upon the inhibition of their growth, which increases population survivability.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing heterogeneous populations and mathematical modeling.

claim: The transition to peptide absorption occurs more likely in the late stage of cell division cycles.
source: This transition occurs more likely in the late stage of cell division cycles.
evidence: This is supported by single-cell data showing correlation between cell size and translocation time.

claim: Cultures with high cell density exhibit two distinct subpopulations: a non-growing population that absorb peptides and a growing population that survive owing to the sequestration of the AMPs by others.
source: Cultures with high cell density exhibit two distinct subpopulations: a non-growing population that absorb peptides and a growing population that survive owing to the sequestration of the AMPs by others.
evidence: This is directly observed in single-cell microscopy experiments with sub-MIC concentrations.

claim: The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of LL37 increases with cell density even in dilute cultures.
source: the increase of the minimum inhibitory concentration with cell density (even in dilute cultures)
evidence: This is demonstrated by microplate assays showing MIC dependence on inoculum size.

claim: Sub-lethal dosages of LL37 peptides introduce extensive lag in growth.
source: the extensive lag in growth introduced by sub-lethal dosages of LL37 peptides.
evidence: This is observed in microplate experiments and reproduced by mathematical modeling.

claim: AMPs are part of the first line of defense against invading microbes in multicellular systems.
source: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are natural amino-acid based antibiotics that are part of the first line of defense against invading microbes in multicellular systems (Zasloff, 2002; Brogden, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In humans, AMPs are found in many organs that are in contact with the outside world, including airways, skin, and the urinary tract.
source: In humans, AMPs are found in many organs that are in contact with the outside world, including airways, skin, and the urinary tract (Hancock and Lehrer, 1998; Zasloff, 2002; Brogden, 2005; Jenssen et al., 2006; Ganz, 2003; Epand and Vogel, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: AMPs typically contain less than 50 amino acids.
source: The short sequence of the AMPs (typically <50 amino acids)
evidence: This is established knowledge about AMP structure.

claim: Structures of AMPs exhibit two common motifs: cationic charge and amphiphilic form.
source: Structures of AMPs exhibit two common motifs: cationic charge and amphiphilic form (Zasloff, 2002; Brogden, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The cationic charge enables AMPs to attack bacteria, enclosed in negatively charged membranes, rather than mammalian cells, which possess electrically neutral membranes.
source: The cationic charge enables them to attack bacteria, enclosed in negatively charged membranes, rather than mammalian cells, which possess electrically neutral membranes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about AMP selectivity based on electrostatic interactions.

claim: The amphiphilic structure allows AMPs to penetrate into the lipid membrane structures.
source: The amphiphilic structure allows AMPs to penetrate into the lipid membrane structures (Matsuzaki et al., 1995; Shai, 1999; Ludtke et al., 1996; Heller et al., 2000; Taheri-Araghi and Ha, 2007; Huang, 2000; Yang et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The density of cells in a culture can alter the activity of AMPs through distributions among different cells.
source: Specifically, it was suggested by Matsuzaki and Castanho et al. that the density of cells in a culture can alter the activity of AMPs through distributions among different cells (Matsuzaki, 1999; Melo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cell density has a decisive role on the effectivity of antimicrobial peptides.
source: Experimental investigations using bacteria and red blood cells by Stella and Wimley groups (Savini et al., 2017; Starr et al., 2016) directly demonstrated the decisive role of cell density on the effectivity of antimicrobial peptides.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: For some antibiotics, including AMPs, the MIC is dependent on the cell density.
source: For some antibiotics, including AMPs, the MIC is dependent on the cell density.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the inoculum effect.

claim: In dilute cultures, MICs have been reported to reach a plateau independent of cell density.
source: However, in dilute cultures, MICs have been reported to reach a plateau independent of cell density (Savini et al., 2017; Starr et al., 2016; Udekwu et al., 2009; Artemova et al., 2015), unless the cell population becomes so small that stochastic single-cell effects become important (Coates et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The inhibition of growth of E. coli cells was followed by the translocation of a large number of AMPs into the cytoplasmic compartment of cells.
source: By tracking a dye-tagged version of LL37 peptide (5-FAM-LC-LL37, AnaSpec), we found that the inhibition of growth of E. coli cells was followed by the translocation of a large number of AMPs into the cytoplasmic compartment of cells, thus reducing the peptide concentration in the culture, which works in favor of other cells.
evidence: This is supported by single-cell fluorescence microscopy data.

claim: The translocation of AMPs into cells reduces the peptide concentration in the culture, which works in favor of other cells.
source: we found that the inhibition of growth of E. coli cells was followed by the translocation of a large number of AMPs into the cytoplasmic compartment of cells, thus reducing the peptide concentration in the culture, which works in favor of other cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of peptide absorption and the survival of subpopulations.

claim: Below the MIC, peptide is absorbed by only a fraction of cells, leaving an inadequate amount of AMPs to inhibit the growth of remaining cells.
source: Below the MIC, peptide is absorbed by only a fraction of cells, leaving an inadequate amount of AMPs to inhibit the growth of remaining cells.
evidence: This is supported by single-cell microscopy observations of heterogeneous populations.

claim: Cultures with sub-MIC concentrations of dye-tagged LL37 peptides exhibit a heterogenous population combining non-growing cells containing many LL37 peptides and growing cells without LL37 peptides.
source: We have directly observed that cultures with sub-MIC concentrations of dye-tagged LL37 peptides (5-FAM-LC-LL37) exhibit a heterogenous population combining non-growing cells containing many LL37 peptides and growing cells without LL37 peptides.
evidence: This is directly observed in single-cell microscopy experiments.

claim: The increase in MIC with cell density represents one order of magnitude increase, which can be critical in medical applications.
source: This is one order of magnitude increase in the MIC value, which can be critical in medical applications.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing MIC changes and speculation about medical implications.

claim: Sub-MIC concentrations of LL37 peptides introduce an extended lag phase up to several hours.
source: An interesting feature observed in the results was the extended lag phase, up to several hours, introduced by the sub-MIC concentrations of LL37 peptides (see Figure 1C).
evidence: This is observed in microplate experiments and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The peptides are stable over the duration of the experiment.
source: We tested and confirmed the stability of peptides over the duration of the experiment (Appendix 2).
evidence: This is confirmed by experimental testing described in Appendix 2.

claim: The growth delay behavior is attributed to heterogenous cell death, where the growth of a fraction of the cells is inhibited, while the rest of the cells recover the normal population growth after a time delay that is correlated to the number of dead cells.
source: Hence, we hypothesized that this behavior was attributed to heterogenous cell death, where the growth of a fraction of the cells is inhibited, while the rest of the cells recover the normal population growth after a time delay that is correlated to the number of dead cells.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from the observed growth patterns.

claim: In the microplate experiments, direct cell-to-cell interactions are minimal as the cells are on average over 50 μm apart from each other.
source: In the microplate experiments, direct cell-to-cell interactions are minimal as the cells are on average over 50 μm apart from each other (corresponding to inoculum size in Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is calculated from the inoculum sizes used in the experiments.

claim: All the electrostatic interactions are completely shielded in the microplate experiments.
source: All the electrostatic interactions are completely shielded.
evidence: This is inferred from the large cell-to-cell distances and knowledge of electrostatic screening in solution.

claim: The amount of absorbed AMPs in cultures with AMP concentrations higher than the MIC can well exceed the required amount of AMPs to kill a cell.
source: Note that the amount of absorbed AMPs in cultures with AMP concentrations higher than the MIC can well exceed the required amount of AMPs to kill a cell.
evidence: This is inferred from the measurements of absorbed AMPs.

claim: The inhibition of growth is followed by a rapid translocation of peptides into target cells, as quantified by a jump in the cell's fluorescent signal.
source: By analyzing 383 cells, we observed that the inhibition of growth is followed by a rapid translocation of peptides into target cells, as quantified by a jump in the cell's fluorescent signal (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is observed in single-cell fluorescence microscopy experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Fluorescent signals showed a bimodal distribution over the course of the experiment.
source: As a result, fluorescent signals showed a bimodal distribution over the course of the experiment.
evidence: This is observed in the fluorescence intensity histograms from single-cell experiments.

claim: A large degree of temporal, cell-to-cell heterogeneity was observed as the peptide translocation time varied for about 30 min for different cells.
source: A large degree of temporal, cell-to-cell heterogeneity was also observed as the peptide translocation time varied for about 30 min for different cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is observed in single-cell tracking data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The fluorescent signal remained high after translocation confirming retention of peptides in the cells.
source: The fluorescent signal remained high after translocation confirming retention of peptides in the cells.
evidence: This is observed in time-lapse fluorescence microscopy data.

claim: The signal strength is reduced in the regions with densely packed fluorophores.
source: As such, the signal strength is reduced in the regions with densely packed fluorophores (Swiecicki et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on knowledge of fluorophore self-quenching and supported by a citation.

claim: The translocation happens shortly after the inhibition of growth and shrinkage of the cell.
source: The average behavior (white line) of the collapse shows that the translocation happens shortly after the inhibition of growth and shrinkage of the cell.
evidence: This is observed in the analysis of instantaneous growth rate data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: E. coli cells exhibited a binary physiological state over the course of the peptide action in terms of growth rate and peptide uptake.
source: As a whole, E. coli cells exhibited a binary physiological state over the course of the peptide action in terms of growth rate and peptide uptake.
evidence: This is observed in single-cell microscopy data and quantified in Figure 2D.

claim: Cells are found to be in either of these distinct states: (1) growing, with no significant peptide uptake; and (2) non-growing, followed by an abrupt peptide uptake.
source: That is, the cells were found to be in either of these distinct states: (1) growing, with no significant peptide uptake; and (2) non-growing, followed by an abrupt peptide uptake.
evidence: This is observed in single-cell microscopy data.

claim: At the peptide concentration of 10 μM (above the MIC) all cells were initially in state (1) and then transitioned to state (2) within one generation.
source: At the peptide concentration of 10 μM (above the MIC) all cells were initially in state (1) and then transitioned to state (2) within one generation.
evidence: This is observed in single-cell microscopy experiments with above-MIC concentrations.

claim: At sub-MIC concentration (4.0 μM), most individual cells grew to form micro-colonies.
source: Hence, we proceeded with single-cell experiments as noted above with a sole modification of using a lower, sub-MIC concentration of 5-FAM-LC-LL37 (4.0 μM for the dye-tagged peptide). As such, most individual cells grew to form micro-colonies.
evidence: This is observed in single-cell microscopy experiments with sub-MIC concentrations.

claim: Phenotypic heterogeneity was observed in the isogenic population of cells in each micro-colony.
source: The striking observation was the phenotypic heterogeneity in the isogenic population of cells in each micro-colony (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is observed in single-cell microscopy experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: As a colony expanded, growth of some cells was inhibited and peptides translocated into them.
source: As a colony expanded, growth of some cells was inhibited and peptides translocated into them.
evidence: This is observed in time-lapse microscopy of micro-colonies.

claim: At sub-MIC the transition occurred for only a fraction of the cells.
source: The difference is that at sub-MIC the transition occurred for only a fraction of the cells.
evidence: This is observed in single-cell microscopy experiments with sub-MIC concentrations.

claim: The relative size of the colonies initially increased exponentially until the appearance of non-growing cells.
source: Analysis of 13 separate micro-colonies, consisting of a total of 280 cells (over the course of the experiment), showed that the relative size of the colonies initially increased exponentially until the appearance of non-growing cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is observed in analysis of micro-colony growth shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The fluorescence intensity of non-growing cells showed an abrupt transition with comparable relative changes in the signal, which suggests that a similar number of peptides are taken by each cell.
source: The fluorescence intensity of non-growing cells showed an abrupt transition, as in the case of above MIC cultures, with comparable relative changes in the signal, which suggests that a similar number of peptides are taken by each cell (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is observed in fluorescence intensity measurements shown in Figure 3C and inferred from the similarity of signal changes.

claim: The absorbed AMPs are bound to the membrane as well as to the cytoplasm of the cell and are not recycled to attack other cells.
source: These AMPs are bound to the membrane as well as to the cytoplasm of the cell and are not recycled to attack other cells.
evidence: This is an assumption in the mathematical model based on the observation of peptide retention.

claim: The discrepancy between the two estimates might arise from the fact that cells can divide several times before they stop growing and absorb peptides.
source: This discrepancy might arise from the fact that cells can divide several times before they stop growing and absorb peptides, which was neglected in the estimate from the colorimetric measurements.
evidence: This is speculation about the reason for the discrepancy between measurements.

claim: The predictions of the model agree reasonably well with experimental results for the growth delay of population.
source: The predictions of our model agree reasonably well with experimental results for the growth delay of population (see Figure 4D), given the simplicity of the model.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of model predictions with experimental data in Figure 4D.

claim: Deviations between model and experiment likely originate from the fact that cell doubling times are scattered, while the model assumes a fixed cell doubling time of 23 min.
source: Deviations likely originate from the fact that cell doubling times are scattered (Figure 1D), while our model assumes a fixed cell doubling time of 23 min.
evidence: This is speculation about the source of deviations between model and experiment.

claim: Due to the exponential growth, the growth delay is highly sensitive to the cell doubling time.
source: Due to the exponential growth, the growth delay is highly sensitive to the cell doubling time.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of exponential growth dynamics.

claim: A negative correlation was observed between peptide translocation time and initial cell length, indicating that small cells can resist the action of AMPs and they continue growing until a later time point.
source: A negative correlation was observed between peptide translocation time and initial cell length, indicating that small cells can resist the action of AMPs and they continue growing until a later time point (Figure 5A left panel).
evidence: This is observed in single-cell data shown in Figure 5A and inferred from the correlation.

claim: Cell length at translocation time did not show any correlation with the translocation time.
source: In contrast, cell length at translocation time did not show any correlation with the translocation time (Figure 5A right panel).
evidence: This is observed in single-cell data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The action of 5-FAM-LC-LL37 is cell-cycle and cell-age dependent.
source: This clearly demonstrated that the action of 5-FAM-LC-LL37 is cell-cycle and cell-age dependent.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between initial cell length and translocation time.

claim: LL37 peptides were observed to first bind to the septum of dividing cells.
source: This seems in agreement with the findings made by the Weisshaar lab, where LL37 peptides were observed to first bind to the septum of dividing cells. Thus, the higher chance to act on larger, dividing cells, as opposed to small growing cells (Sochacki et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: LL37 peptides preferentially bind to membranes with negative Gaussian curvature, a geometry that can be found in the septum of rod shaped microorganisms.
source: Among various possibilities, the Wong lab has shown that LL37 peptides preferentially bind to membranes with negative Gaussian curvature, a geometry that can be found in the septum of rod shaped microorganisms (Yang et al., 2008; Schmidt et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Under sub-MIC concentrations, absorption of AMPs led to the emergence of two distinct subpopulations in an isogenic bacterial culture: a group of cells that retain peptides after their growth is inhibited and a group of surviving cells that grow owing to the reduction of the 'free' peptide concentration by the other group.
source: In this work, we discovered an unexpected absorption and retention of an antimicrobial peptide (LL37 and the dye-tagged analogue, 5-FAM-LC-LL37) in E. coli cells, which under sub-MIC concentrations led to the emergence of two distinct subpopulations in an isogenic bacterial culture: a group of cells that retain peptides after their growth is inhibited and a group of surviving cells that grow owing to the reduction of the 'free' peptide concentration by the other group.
evidence: This is observed in single-cell microscopy experiments.

claim: This 'passive cooperation' is an interesting feature of an E. coli culture where cells do not have any form of active communication.
source: This 'passive cooperation' is an interesting feature of an E. coli culture where cells do not have any form of active communication, unlike ion-channel based cooperation in Bacillus subtilis biofilms (Prindle et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the observations and contrasted with active communication in other bacteria.

claim: A distinct feature of the action of AMPs is its collective nature, where a large number of AMPs are required to first bind to and then disrupt the cell membranes to kill the cell.
source: At the cellular and molecular scales, a distinct feature of the action of AMPs is its collective nature, where a large number of AMPs are required to first bind to and then disrupt the cell membranes to kill the cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about AMP mechanism of action.

claim: The temporal and cell-to-cell heterogeneity in the peptide absorption into E. coli cells goes beyond the membrane binding.
source: Utilizing live, single-cell microscopy, we observed the temporal and cell-to-cell heterogeneity in the peptide absorption into E. coli cells, which goes beyond the membrane binding.
evidence: This is observed in single-cell microscopy experiments showing peptide translocation into the cytoplasm.

claim: The inoculum effect in the case of LL37 pepides arises from the retention of these peptides in target cells.
source: The integration of the population and single-cell data, combined with the theoretical modeling, presented in this work, provides strong evidence that the inoculum effect in the case of LL37 pepides arises from the retention of these peptides in target cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the integration of experimental data and mathematical modeling.

claim: The picture at the single-cell level is simple and binary, consistent in cultures with above-MIC and sub-MIC concentrations of AMPs: occurrence of growth inhibition depends on the free peptide concentration and is followed by an abrupt, permanent translocation of peptides into the target cells.
source: Despite the seeming complexity of the partitioning of LL37 peptides in a population of bacterial cells, the picture at the single-cell level is simple and binary, consistent in cultures with above-MIC and sub-MIC concentrations of AMPs: occurrence of growth inhibition depends on the free peptide concentration and is followed by an abrupt, permanent translocation of peptides into the target cells.
evidence: This is concluded from single-cell microscopy observations.

claim: The large number of absorbed peptides raises the question of which molecules inside of the cells are interacting with LL37 peptides.
source: Yet, this large number raises the question of which molecules inside of the cells are interacting with LL37 peptides.
evidence: This is a question raised based on the observation of large numbers of absorbed peptides.

claim: The negative charge of DNA as well as some proteins can provide binding sites for LL37 peptides.
source: The negative charge of DNA as well as some proteins can provide binding sites for LL37 peptides.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of electrostatic interactions.

claim: Translocation of 5-FAM-LC-LL37 peptides into mini-cells showed qualitatively similar absorption and retention as seen in regular cells.
source: Translocation of 5-FAM-LC-LL37 peptides into mini-cells showed qualitatively similar absorption and retention as seen in regular cells (Figure 6B), which suggests the presence of significant interactions of AMPs with the intracellular content other than DNA.
evidence: This is observed in experiments with mini-cells shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The rate at which AMPs are absorbed into the mini-cells is slower than that in the neighboring mother cells with DNA content, perhaps indicating the role of the negative charge of DNA.
source: Yet, the rate at which AMPs are absorbed into the mini-cells is slower than that in the neighboring mother cells with DNA content (Figure 6B), perhaps indicating the role of the negative charge of DNA.
evidence: This is observed in experiments with mini-cells shown in Figure 6B and speculation about the role of DNA.

claim: The strong absorption of peptides into the cytoplasmic area raises questions on the nature and impact of this intercellular binding.
source: First, the strong absorption of peptides into the cytoplasmic area raises questions on the nature and impact of this intercellular binding: what specific proteins and domains are peptides binding to? How does the peptide binding perturb the protein functions?
evidence: These are questions raised based on the observations.

claim: The population survivability as a result of peptide absorption raises questions on the evolutionary dynamics of this phenomena.
source: Second, the population survivability as a result of peptide absorption raises questions on the evolutionary dynamics of this phenomena: how do E. coli cells evolve to achieve this cooperative fit? How does this phenomena affect multi-species cultures with prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms?
evidence: These are questions raised based on the observations.

claim: Considering the peptide absorption into the target cells, AMP concentration should not be assumed the only key factor, but the rate of the expression of the AMPs by the host is also decisive in determining the effectivity of AMPs.
source: Considering the peptide absorption into the target cells, AMP concentration should not be assumed the only key factor, but the rate of the expression of the AMPs by the host is also decisive in determining the effectivity of AMPs.
evidence: This is speculation about the implications of the findings for AMP activity in hosts.

claim: The expression rate competes with the rate of absorption of the AMPs in the bacterial cells.
source: The expression rate competes with the rate of absorption of the AMPs in the bacterial cells.
evidence: This is speculation about the dynamics of AMP activity in hosts.

claim: The strain used is a derivative of E. coli K12 strain NCM3722.
source: In this work, we used derivatives of a prototrophic Escherichia coli K12 strain, NCM3722, that was constructed, sequenced, and extensively tested by Kustu and Jun labs (Soupene et al., 2003; Brown and Jun, 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the bacterial strain used, supported by citations.

claim: The average generation time of the E. coli strain used in this study was 23 min in RDM at 37°C.
source: The average generation time of the E. coli strain used in this study was 23 min in RDM at 37°C.
evidence: This is an experimental measurement of the growth rate.

claim: The net peptide content of the purchased material was quantified at 75% by elemental analysis of the carbon, hydrogen, and nitrogen content (CHN analysis).
source: The net peptide content of the purchased material was quantified at 75% by elemental analysis of the carbon, hydrogen, and nitrogen content (CHN analysis) through the manufacturing company.
evidence: This is information about the peptide purity from the manufacturer.

claim: 1 μg/mL of cephalexin results in the 17% increase in the length of the newborn cells, from 3.37 μm to 3.96 μm, without any appreciable change of the growth rate.
source: Our measurements using the microfluidic 'mother machine' (Wang et al., 2010) also showed that 1 μg/mL of cephalexin results in the 17% increase in the length of the newborn cells (Figure 5B), from 3.37 μm to 3.96 μm, without any appreciable change of the growth rate.
evidence: This is measured experimentally using microfluidic mother machine.

claim: The model predicts two different outcomes depending on the initial concentrations of bacteria and AMPs: (1) The population of bacteria goes extinct for a sufficiently large concentration of AMPs, that is above MIC; (2) The population of bacteria can recover in a low concentration of AMPs, that is below MIC.
source: This model predicts two different outcomes (see Figure 4B) depending on the initial concentrations of bacteria and AMPs: (1) The population of bacteria goes extinct for a sufficiently large concentration of AMPs, that is above MIC; (2) The population of bacteria can recover in a low concentration of AMPs, that is below MIC.
evidence: This is a prediction from the mathematical model shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Only binding or degradation of AMPs of the same order of magnitude (10^8) per individual cells can lead to the inoculum effect.
source: At such a high ratio, only binding or degradation of AMPs of the same order of magnitude per individual cells can lead to the inoculum effect (Starr et al., 2016; Savini et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the ratio of AMPs to cells and supported by citations.
